introLesson.title: Introduction to Julius Caesar

sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, married Anne Hathaway in 1582 and had three children, Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith. By the early 1590s he was writing and acting in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, the company that built the Globe on the south bank of the Thames in 1599. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays, including histories of English kings and tragedies drawn from Roman history, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. His fellow actors collected his plays in the First Folio of 1623.
sections.historicalContext: Julius Caesar dates from 1599, the year the Globe opened; a Swiss traveller, Thomas Platter, recorded seeing a play about Caesar at a Thameside playhouse on 21 September 1599. Shakespeare's source was Plutarch's Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans in Thomas North's English translation (1579), which he followed closely, sometimes almost word for word. The historical Caesar was stabbed in the Senate house on the Ides of March (15 March) 44 BCE by senators led by Brutus and Cassius; Antony and Octavius defeated them at Philippi in 42 BCE. For English audiences in 1599 the story had urgent echoes: Queen Elizabeth I was old, had no heir, and the question of who would rule next, and whether resisting a ruler could ever be justified, was dangerous to discuss openly.

publicationAndReception.publication: The play was first printed in the First Folio (1623), in an unusually clean text that is thought to come from a theatrical manuscript. It is the first of Shakespeare's Roman tragedies drawn from Plutarch, followed by Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus.
publicationAndReception.then: It was popular from the start: the poet Leonard Digges, in verses printed in 1640, recalled audiences "ravish'd" by the quarrel scene between Brutus and Cassius while other plays emptied the house. It remained in the repertory after the Restoration and was among the most performed Shakespeare plays in the eighteenth century.
publicationAndReception.now: The play is a school standard, partly because it has little sexual content and centres on rhetoric and politics. Productions often make it about modern power: Orson Welles's 1937 Mercury Theatre staging dressed Caesar as a fascist dictator; Joseph Mankiewicz's 1953 film starred Marlon Brando as Antony; the Public Theater's 2017 Shakespeare in the Park production, with a Caesar resembling a contemporary president, provoked national controversy and lost sponsors. Critics debate who the hero is, Caesar or Brutus, and whether the assassination is presented as justified.

sections.overview: Julius Caesar returns to Rome in triumph, and some senators fear he will make himself king. Cassius sets out to persuade the respected Brutus to join a conspiracy. The play follows what they decide, what happens on the Ides of March, and how words, especially the speeches at Caesar's funeral, change the course of Rome.

sections.whyItMatters: The play asks questions every democracy faces: when is it right to resist a leader, and what happens when a crowd can be swayed by a good speech? It is also the best training ground in literature for analyzing persuasion, a skill students need every day.

spoilerOverview.text: The conspirators stab Caesar in the Capitol. Brutus lets Antony speak at the funeral; Antony's oration turns the crowd, and the conspirators flee. Antony, Octavius and Lepidus draw up a death list. Brutus and Cassius quarrel and reconcile; Portia has killed herself; Caesar's ghost visits Brutus. At Philippi Cassius has himself killed after misreading a report, and Brutus runs on his own sword; Antony calls him "the noblest Roman of them all."

passage.quote: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings
passage.use: Cassius's line, among the most quoted in Shakespeare: a claim that people, not fate, are responsible. Ask students to watch whether the play agrees.

flags: Platter does not name the playhouse; most scholars identify it as the newly built Globe.

Plutarch reports that Caesar spoke words to Brutus as he died (in Greek, "You too, child?" in some sources); the Latin "Et tu, Brute?" is not in Plutarch and appears in earlier English plays. Do not present it as Caesar's historical last words.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings” slowly and put it in my own words: Cassius tells Brutus that their low position is their own fault, not the stars'. Next, craft. I notice the contrast between "stars" (fate) and "ourselves" (choice). The strongest word is “underlings”: it is a contemptuous word for inferiors, which stings Brutus's pride. Then, effect. What is Cassius arguing to Brutus? My answer: Cassius urges Brutus to act against Caesar, claiming free will; the line shows his skill at manipulation and introduces the play's question of fate versus choice.

segments.script: Shakespeare wrote Julius Caesar in 1599, when Queen Elizabeth was old and had no heir, and Londoners feared civil war over the succession. introLesson.objective: Students will explain, in a 3-sentence exit ticket, how one fact about William Shakespeare's life or times connects to power, ambition and tyranny in “Julius Caesar”, and will set up a reading journal with a prediction and a question for each of 3 themes (power, ambition and tyranny, honor and self-deception, rhetoric and persuasion).

lessonPlan.title: Julius Caesar unit
lessonPlan.author: William Shakespeare
lessonPlan.edition: First Folio (1623) text as edited by Standard Ebooks
lessonPlan.editionNote: Julius Caesar survives only in the 1623 First Folio; it was first performed in 1599 at the new Globe. The reading text is the Standard Ebooks edition, divided into the conventional 18 scenes (plus the cast list). Shakespeare's main source was Thomas North's 1579 English translation of Plutarch's Lives. Cite act, scene and line from this edition.
lessonPlan.gradeBand: Grades 9–10 (scales to graduate via rigor levels)

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Julius Caesar.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Julius Caesar: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

lessonPlan.middleSchoolTrack: Scaffolded-support track (grade-9 floor): students work from teacher-selected passages with scaffolds, sentence starters and partial-credit probes.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Julius Caesar has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to power, ambition and tyranny.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Julius Caesar. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to power, ambition and tyranny.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Julius Caesar.

essentialQuestions: What does Julius Caesar suggest about power, ambition and tyranny?
What does Julius Caesar suggest about honor and self-deception?
What does Julius Caesar suggest about rhetoric and persuasion?
What does Julius Caesar suggest about public versus private self?
What does Julius Caesar suggest about fate, omens and free will?
objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

wholeBookTest.title: Julius Caesar: unit test

items.prompt: In the line “Artemidorus of Cnidos, a teacher of rhetoric”, what does “rhetoric” most nearly mean?
What does the letter tell Caesar security gives way to?
In the line “If thou beest not immortal, look about you: security gives way to conspiracy.”, what does “security” most nearly mean?
options: overconfidence; a false sense of safety

items.prompt: What does Artemidorus's letter contain?

In the line “There are no tricks in plain and simple faith; But hollow men, like horses hot at hand, Make gallant show and promise of their mettle; But when they should endure the bloody spur, They fall their crests, and, like…”, what does “deceitful” most nearly mean?
options: a wreath worn as a sign of victory
to stand over with legs wide apart

items.prompt: Where does Brutus want to argue with Cassius?
In the line “Thou hast described A hot friend cooling: ever note, Lucilius, When love begins to sicken and decay, It useth an enforced ceremony.”, what does “ceremony” most nearly mean?
options: shallow water where ships run aground

items.prompt: In the line “Free from the bondage you are in, Messala: The conquerors can but make a fire of him; For Brutus only overcame himself, And no man else hath honour by his death.”, what does “conquerors” most nearly mean?
options: a person who joins a secret plot

items.prompt: In the line “Sit thee down, Clitus: slaying is the word; It is a deed in fashion.”, what does “slaying” most nearly mean?
options: to stand over with legs wide apart

items.prompt: What does Brutus say to Caesar as he dies?
options: He will see him in Rome
He killed Caesar with less good will than himself

items.prompt: Who holds the sword for Brutus?
What does this passage most clearly show? “These growing feathers pluck’d from Caesar’s wing / Will make him fly an ordinary pitch” (Act I, Scene I, Flavius)
options: The tribunes' metaphor of limiting Caesar's power.
Listed among the conspirators; he has more lines than anyone.

items.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Act III, Scene III”?
options: The tribunes and the fickle crowd
The cast and world of the play

items.prompt: What does this passage most clearly show? “the elements / So mix’d in him that Nature might stand up / And say to all the world ‘This was a man” (Act V, Scene V, Antony)
options: The title character, who will die halfway through.
Antony praises Brutus as the balanced, ideal man, even in defeat.

items.prompt: Which literary element does this describe in “Dramatis Personae”? Caesar, the title character, dies in Act III; the cast list does not tell us that Brutus has the most lines.
Which literary element does this describe in “Act II, Scene III”? Artemidorus reads his warning letter to the audience.
Which literary element does this describe in “Act IV, Scene I”? Antony, Octavius and Lepidus draw up a death list; Antony mocks Lepidus behind his back.

The claim is therefore a strong reading, not a complete one, and a careful answer says where it stops applying.

This develops honour and idealism: Brutus's honour recognized. The words “noblest” and “them” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Antony calls him "the noblest Roman of them all," and Brutus's last words, "I kill'd not thee with half so good a will," admit his reluctance.

scoringGuide.full: A nuanced thesis; close reading of diction, syntax or form in two or more passages; synthesis across sections; acknowledges a competing reading and answers it.
scoringGuide.partial: 4: strong analysis without a competing reading; 3: analysis of one passage; 2: summary with some analysis; 1: claim only.

answerKey.answer: brother

Brutus's decision. The evidence is “It must be by his death” (Act II, Scene I, Brutus). This develops honour and idealism: Brutus wants a clean, almost ritual killing: "sacrificers, but not butchers.".
Preventive reasoning. The evidence is “And therefore think him as a serpent’s egg / Which, hatch’d, would, as his kind, grow mischievous, / And kill him in the shell” (Act II, Scene I, Brutus).

His case rests on speculation about Caesar's future, not facts. The evidence is “It must be by his death” (Act II, Scene I, Brutus) — Brutus's decision. This develops honour and idealism: Brutus wants a clean, almost ritual killing: "sacrificers, but not butchers.".
It punctures Caesar's godlike self-image: he is mortal and must take care. The evidence is “Caesar, beware of Brutus; take heed of Cassius” (Act II, Scene III, Artemidorus) — The letter.
The letter. The evidence is “Caesar, beware of Brutus; take heed of Cassius” (Act II, Scene III, Artemidorus). This develops fate and omens: one more warning that fails.

The proscription. The evidence is “These many, then, shall die; their names are prick’d” (Act IV, Scene I, Antony). This develops power and ambition: the new rulers are as ruthless as the conspirators feared Caesar would be.

Antony on Lepidus. The evidence is “This is a slight unmeritable man, / Meet to be sent on errands” (Act IV, Scene I, Antony). This develops power and ambition: the new rulers are as ruthless as the conspirators feared Caesar would be.
As a matter of tools and advantage; allies are used and discarded. The evidence is “These many, then, shall die; their names are prick’d” (Act IV, Scene I, Antony) — The proscription.
Brutus and Cassius at odds
Brutus's concern for appearance.
Urgent, hopeful, perhaps rash: Brutus's hope. The evidence is “sudden push gives them the overthrow” (Act V, Scene II, Brutus). This develops fate and omens: Brutus's haste.
Brutus. The evidence is “O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet” (Act V, Scene III, Brutus). This develops fate and omens: Caesar's spirit seems to win.
Lucilius's disguise. The evidence is “Brutus, my country’s friend; know me for Brutus” (Act V, Scene IV, Brutus). This develops friendship and loyalty: Lucilius's loyalty.
Antony praises Brutus as the balanced, ideal man, even in defeat.
The death of Brutus
Characterization

Cassius's image of Caesar's size and his own smallness. The evidence is “Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus” (Act I, Scene II, Cassius). This develops power and ambition: Cassius argues that men, not fate, make their own subjection. The words “bestride” and “narrow” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
Soliloquy

Decius's flattery. The evidence is “This dream is all amiss interpreted” (Act II, Scene II, Decius). This develops fate and omens: Caesar ignores the omens out of pride. The words “interpreted” and “dream” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Envy kills virtue. The evidence is “My heart laments that virtue cannot live / Out of the teeth of emulation” (Act II, Scene III). This develops fate and omens: one more warning that fails. The words “emulation” and “laments” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

"If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayst live," he says, and the audience knows Caesar will not read it. The evidence is “If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayst live” (Act II, Scene III) — Artemidorus's hope. This develops fate and omens: one more warning that fails.

She says "I have a man's mind, but a woman's might," wanting to act but unable. The evidence is “I have a man’s mind, but a woman’s might” (Act II, Scene IV, Portia) — Portia's frustration. This develops honour and idealism: Portia's suffering shows the cost of political secrets.

Antony's prophecy of civil war. The evidence is “Cry ‘Havoc,’ and let slip the dogs of war” (Act III, Scene I, Antony). This develops power and ambition: Caesar's final speech is his most arrogant: he claims to be "constant as the northern star.". The words “slip” and “dogs” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

Brutus rests his case on honour ("I loved Rome more"), so Antony repeats "Brutus is an honourable man" until the phrase sounds false, while showing the wounds and the will to move the crowd. The evidence is “For Brutus is an honourable man” (Act III, Scene II, Antony), which shows the repeated ironic refrain. This develops rhetoric and persuasion: the scene is a masterclass in ethos, pathos and logos.

The mob's logic. The evidence is “It is no matter, his name’s Cinna” (Act III, Scene III, Fourth Citizen). This develops rhetoric and persuasion: the crowd Antony stirred becomes a lynch mob. The words “matter” and “name” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.

They begin with "These many, then, shall die," and Antony plans to "cut off some charge in legacies" from the will he used to win the crowd. The evidence is “we shall determine / How to cut off some charge in legacies” (Act IV, Scene I, Antony) — Reducing the will. This develops power and ambition: the new rulers are as ruthless as the conspirators feared Caesar would be.

Brutus's hope. The evidence is “sudden push gives them the overthrow” (Act V, Scene II, Brutus). This develops fate and omens: Brutus's haste. The words “overthrow” and “sudden” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
"Let them set on at once," he orders. The evidence is “Let them set on at once” (Act V, Scene II, Brutus) — Haste. This develops fate and omens: Brutus's haste.
Pacing
Act V, Scene III
Characterization

Antony's respect. The evidence is “I had rather have / Such men my friends than enemies” (Act V, Scene IV, Antony). This develops friendship and loyalty: Lucilius's loyalty. The words “enemies” and “friends” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect.
Act V, Scene V

Listed among the conspirators; he has more lines than anyone. The evidence is “Marcus Brutus” (Dramatis Personae). This develops power and ambition: every group is defined by its relation to Caesar's power. Caesar, Antony and Octavius head one list, and Brutus, Cassius and the other conspirators another, so the play begins as a map of loyalty and opposition.

Marullus's contempt for the crowd. The evidence is “You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things” (Act I, Scene I, Marullus). This develops rhetoric and persuasion: the crowd is fickle, the central fact the funeral orations will exploit. The words “senseless” and “stones” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Marullus reminds them they once cheered Pompey and calls them "you blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things," and the tribunes plan to pluck "growing feathers" from Caesar's wing.

Caesar reads Cassius accurately. The evidence is “Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look; / He thinks too much: such men are dangerous” (Act I, Scene II, Caesar). This develops power and ambition: Cassius argues that men, not fate, make their own subjection. The words “dangerous” and “thinks” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He says Caesar "doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus" while others are "underlings," and insists "the fault ... is not in our stars, / But in ourselves," urging Brutus to act.

Cassius's argument for action. The evidence is “The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings” (Act I, Scene II, Cassius). This develops power and ambition: Cassius argues that men, not fate, make their own subjection. The words “underlings” and “ourselves” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He says Caesar "doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus" while others are "underlings," and insists "the fault ... is not in our stars, / But in ourselves," urging Brutus to act.

His resolve to die rather than live under tyranny. The evidence is “Cassius from bondage will deliver Cassius” (Act I, Scene III, Cassius). This develops fate and omens: each character reads the omens to suit himself. The words “bondage” and “deliver” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Cicero warns that "men may construe things after their fashion, / Clean from the purpose of the things themselves," and Cassius promptly reads the storm as a sign against Caesar.

Third-person speech. The evidence is “Caesar shall go forth” (Act II, Scene II, Caesar). This develops fate and omens: Caesar ignores the omens out of pride. The words “forth” and “shall” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Decius says the dream is "all amiss interpreted," and Caesar, who calls himself "Caesar" in the third person, goes, insisting the valiant "never taste of death but once.".

Caesar's courage or pride. The evidence is “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once” (Act II, Scene II, Caesar). This develops fate and omens: Caesar ignores the omens out of pride. The words “valiant” and “before” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Decius says the dream is "all amiss interpreted," and Caesar, who calls himself "Caesar" in the third person, goes, insisting the valiant "never taste of death but once.".

Her self-criticism. The evidence is “How hard it is for women to keep counsel” (Act II, Scene IV, Portia). This develops honour and idealism: Portia's suffering shows the cost of political secrets. The words “counsel” and “women” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. She says "I have a man's mind, but a woman's might," wanting to act but unable.

The mob's cruelty. The evidence is “Tear him for his bad verses” (Act III, Scene III, Fourth Citizen). This develops rhetoric and persuasion: the crowd Antony stirred becomes a lynch mob. The words “verses” and “his” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. When he protests "I am Cinna the poet," the mob answers "It is no matter, his name's Cinna" and "Tear him for his bad verses.".

His plea. The evidence is “I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet” (Act III, Scene III, Cinna). This develops rhetoric and persuasion: the crowd Antony stirred becomes a lynch mob. The words “poet” and “the” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. When he protests "I am Cinna the poet," the mob answers "It is no matter, his name's Cinna" and "Tear him for his bad verses.".

Cassius's accusation. The evidence is “Most noble brother, you have done me wrong” (Act IV, Scene II, Cassius). This develops friendship and loyalty: the friendship under strain. The words “brother” and “noble” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Brutus observes that when love "begins to sicken and decay, / It useth an enforced ceremony.".

Brutus on cooling friendship. The evidence is “When love begins to sicken and decay, / It useth an enforced ceremony” (Act IV, Scene II, Brutus). This develops friendship and loyalty: the friendship under strain. The words “enforced” and “ceremony” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Brutus observes that when love "begins to sicken and decay, / It useth an enforced ceremony.".

Brutus's farewell. The evidence is “Forever, and forever, farewell, Cassius” (Act V, Scene I, Brutus). This develops fate and omens: the eagles that followed them have flown, replaced by ravens and kites. The words “farewell” and “forever” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Brutus's "Forever, and forever, farewell, Cassius" is a final goodbye, and Cassius notes "This is my birth-day.".

Urgency. The evidence is “Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills” (Act V, Scene II, Brutus). This develops fate and omens: Brutus's haste. The words “these” and “bills” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. "Let them set on at once," he orders.

Young Cato. The evidence is “I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho” (Act V, Scene IV, Cato). This develops friendship and loyalty: Lucilius's loyalty. The words “son” and “the” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. He cries "know me for Brutus," and Antony says he would "rather have / Such men my friends than enemies.".

Antony judges Brutus the only conspirator who acted for the common good. The evidence is “This was the noblest Roman of them all” (Act V, Scene V, Antony). This develops honour and idealism: Brutus's honour recognized. The words “noblest” and “them” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Antony calls him "the noblest Roman of them all," and Brutus's last words, "I kill'd not thee with half so good a will," admit his reluctance.

middleSchool.label: Scaffolded support
middleSchool.text: Supported track: write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Julius Caesar teaches about power, ambition and tyranny. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how William Shakespeare develops power, ambition and tyranny in Julius Caesar. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how William Shakespeare develops power, ambition and tyranny across Julius Caesar. Trace the idea through at least three scenes and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior

hsSenior.label: HS Senior

ap.label: AP

Do not merely summarize.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior

prompts.text: Analyze how William Shakespeare develops power, ambition and tyranny across Julius Caesar. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Julius Caesar and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to honor and self-deception.
Analyze a central character's choices in Julius Caesar. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether Julius Caesar finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of rhetoric and persuasion. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.

finalPaper.exemplar: The cast list shows a world organized around one man's power. The text makes this visible when it says “Julius Caesar” (Dramatis Personae). Caesar, Antony and Octavius head one list, and Brutus, Cassius and the other conspirators another, so the play begins as a map of loyalty and opposition. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
